title: Binary search
html:
Binary search is a method that allows for quicker search of something by splitting the search interval into two. Its most common application is searching values in sorted arrays, however the splitting idea is crucial in many other typical tasks.

Search in sorted arrays

The most typical problem that leads to the binary search is as follows. You're given a sorted array A0≤A1≤⋯≤An−1A_0 \leq A_1 \leq \dots \leq A_{n-1}A0​≤A1​≤⋯≤An−1​, check if kkk is present within the sequence. The simplest solution would be to check every element one by one and compare it with kkk (a so-called linear search). This approach works in O(n)O(n)O(n), but doesn't utilize the fact that the array is sorted.


Binary search of the value 777 in an array.
The image by AlwaysAngry is distributed under CC BY-SA 4.0 license.

Now assume that we know two indices L<RL < RL<R such that AL≤k≤ARA_L \leq k \leq A_RAL​≤k≤AR​. Because the array is sorted, we can deduce that kkk either occurs among AL,AL+1,…,ARA_L, A_{L+1}, \dots, A_RAL​,AL+1​,…,AR​ or doesn't occur in the array at all. If we pick an arbitrary index MMM such that L<M<RL < M < RL<M<R and check whether kkk is less or greater than AMA_MAM​. We have two possible cases:

  1. AL≤k≤AMA_L \leq k \leq A_MAL​≤k≤AM​. In this case, we reduce the problem from [L,R][L, R][L,R] to [L,M][L, M][L,M];
  2. AM≤k≤ARA_M \leq k \leq A_RAM​≤k≤AR​. In this case, we reduce the problem from [L,R][L, R][L,R] to [M,R][M, R][M,R].

When it is impossible to pick MMM, that is, when R=L+1R = L + 1R=L+1, we directly compare kkk with ALA_LAL​ and ARA_RAR​. Otherwise we would want to pick MMM in such manner that it reduces the active segment to a single element as quickly as possible in the worst case.

Since in the worst case we will always reduce to larger segment of [L,M][L, M][L,M] and [M,R][M, R][M,R]. Thus, in the worst case scenario the reduction would be from R−LR-LR−L to max⁡(M−L,R−M)\max(M-L, R-M)max(M−L,R−M). To minimize this value, we should pick M≈L+R2M \approx \frac{L+R}{2}M≈2L+R​, then

M−L≈R−L2≈R−M.M-L \approx \frac{R-L}{2} \approx R-M.M−L≈2R−L​≈R−M.

In other words, from the worst-case scenario perspective it is optimal to always pick MMM in the middle of [L,R][L, R][L,R] and split it in half. Thus, the active segment halves on each step until it becomes of size 111. So, if the process needs hhh steps, in the end it reduces the difference between RRR and LLL from R−LR-LR−L to R−L2h≈1\frac{R-L}{2^h} \approx 12hR−L​≈1, giving us the equation 2h≈R−L2^h \approx R-L2h≈R−L.

Taking log⁡2\log_2log2​ on both sides, we get h≈log⁡2(R−L)∈O(log⁡n)h \approx \log_2(R-L) \in O(\log n)h≈log2​(R−L)∈O(logn).

Logarithmic number of steps is drastically better than that of linear search. For example, for n≈220≈106n \approx 2^{20} \approx 10^6n≈220≈106 you'd need to make approximately a million operations for linear search, but only around 202020 operations with the binary search.

Lower bound and upper bound

It is often convenient to find the position of the first element that is greater or equal than kkk (called the lower bound of kkk in the array) or the position of the first element that is greater than kkk (called the upper bound of kkk) rather than the exact position of the element.

Together, lower and upper bounds produce a possibly empty half-interval of the array elements that are equal to kkk. To check whether kkk is present in the array it's enough to find its lower bound and check if the corresponding element equates to kkk.

Implementation

The explanation above provides a rough description of the algorithm. For the implementation details, we'd need to be more precise.

We will maintain a pair L<RL < RL<R such that AL≤k<ARA_L \leq k < A_RAL​≤k<AR​. Meaning that the active search interval is [L,R)[L, R)[L,R). We use half-interval here instead of a segment [L,R][L, R][L,R] as it turns out to require less corner case work.

When R=L+1R = L+1R=L+1, we can deduce from definitions above that RRR is the upper bound of kkk. It is convenient to initialize RRR with past-the-end index, that is R=nR=nR=n and LLL with before-the-beginning index, that is L=−1L=-1L=−1. It is fine as long as we never evaluate ALA_LAL​ and ARA_RAR​ in our algorithm directly, formally treating it as AL=−∞A_L = -\inftyAL​=−∞ and AR=+∞A_R = +\inftyAR​=+∞.

Finally, to be specific about the value of MMM we pick, we will stick with M=⌊L+R2⌋M = \lfloor \frac{L+R}{2} \rfloorM=⌊2L+R​⌋.

Then the implementation could look like this:

... // a sorted array is stored as a[0], a[1], ..., a[n-1]
int l = -1, r = n;
while (r - l > 1) {
    int m = (l + r) / 2;
    if (k < a[m]) {
        r = m; // a[l] <= k < a[m] <= a[r]
    } else {
        l = m; // a[l] <= a[m] <= k < a[r]
    }
}

During the execution of the algorithm, we never evaluate neither ALA_LAL​ nor ARA_RAR​, as L<M<RL < M < RL<M<R. In the end, LLL will be the index of the last element that is not greater than kkk (or −1-1−1 if there is no such element) and RRR will be the index of the first element larger than kkk (or nnn if there is no such element).

Note. Calculating m as m = (r + l) / 2 can lead to overflow if l and r are two positive integers, and this error lived about 9 years in JDK as described in the blogpost. Some alternative approaches include e.g. writing m = l + (r - l) / 2 which always works for positive integer l and r, but might still overflow if l is a negative number. If you use C++20, it offers an alternative solution in the form of m = std::midpoint(l, r) which always works correctly.

Search on arbitrary predicate

Let f:{0,1,…,n−1}→{0,1}f : \{0,1,\dots, n-1\} \to \{0, 1\}f:{0,1,…,n−1}→{0,1} be a boolean function defined on 0,1,…,n−10,1,\dots,n-10,1,…,n−1 such that it is monotonously increasing, that is

f(0)≤f(1)≤⋯≤f(n−1).f(0) \leq f(1) \leq \dots \leq f(n-1).f(0)≤f(1)≤⋯≤f(n−1).

The binary search, the way it is described above, finds the partition of the array by the predicate f(M)f(M)f(M), holding the boolean value of k<AMk < A_Mk<AM​ expression. It is possible to use arbitrary monotonous predicate instead of k<AMk < A_Mk<AM​. It is particularly useful when the computation of f(k)f(k)f(k) requires too much time to actually compute it for every possible value. In other words, binary search finds the unique index LLL such that f(L)=0f(L) = 0f(L)=0 and f(R)=f(L+1)=1f(R)=f(L+1)=1f(R)=f(L+1)=1 if such a transition point exists, or gives us L=n−1L = n-1L=n−1 if f(0)=⋯=f(n−1)=0f(0) = \dots = f(n-1) = 0f(0)=⋯=f(n−1)=0 or L=−1L = -1L=−1 if f(0)=⋯=f(n−1)=1f(0) = \dots = f(n-1) = 1f(0)=⋯=f(n−1)=1.

Proof of correctness supposing a transition point exists, that is f(0)=0f(0)=0f(0)=0 and f(n−1)=1f(n-1)=1f(n−1)=1: The implementation maintains the loop invariant f(l)=0,f(r)=1f(l)=0, f(r)=1f(l)=0,f(r)=1. When r−l>1r - l > 1r−l>1, the choice of mmm means r−lr-lr−l will always decrease. The loop terminates when r−l=1r - l = 1r−l=1, giving us our desired transition point.

... // f(i) is a boolean function such that f(0) <= ... <= f(n-1)
int l = -1, r = n;
while (r - l > 1) {
    int m = (l + r) / 2;
    if (f(m)) {
        r = m; // 0 = f(l) < f(m) = 1
    } else {
        l = m; // 0 = f(m) < f(r) = 1
    }
}

Binary search on the answer

Such situation often occurs when we're asked to compute some value, but we're only capable of checking whether this value is at least iii. For example, you're given an array a1,…,ana_1,\dots,a_na1​,…,an​ and you're asked to find the maximum floored average sum

⌊al+al+1+⋯+arr−l+1⌋\left \lfloor \frac{a_l + a_{l+1} + \dots + a_r}{r-l+1} \right\rfloor⌊r−l+1al​+al+1​+⋯+ar​​⌋

among all possible pairs of l,rl,rl,r such that r−l≥xr-l \geq xr−l≥x. One of simple ways to solve this problem is to check whether the answer is at least λ\lambdaλ, that is if there is a pair l,rl, rl,r such that the following is true:

al+al+1+⋯+arr−l+1≥λ.\frac{a_l + a_{l+1} + \dots + a_r}{r-l+1} \geq \lambda.r−l+1al​+al+1​+⋯+ar​​≥λ.

Equivalently, it rewrites as

(al−λ)+(al+1−λ)+⋯+(ar−λ)≥0,(a_l - \lambda) + (a_{l+1} - \lambda) + \dots + (a_r - \lambda) \geq 0,(al​−λ)+(al+1​−λ)+⋯+(ar​−λ)≥0,

so now we need to check whether there is a subarray of a new array ai−λa_i - \lambdaai​−λ of length at least x+1x+1x+1 with non-negative sum, which is doable with some prefix sums.

Continuous search

Let f:R→Rf : \mathbb R \to \mathbb Rf:R→R be a real-valued function that is continuous on a segment [L,R][L, R][L,R].

Without loss of generality assume that f(L)≤f(R)f(L) \leq f(R)f(L)≤f(R). From intermediate value theorem it follows that for any y∈[f(L),f(R)]y \in [f(L), f(R)]y∈[f(L),f(R)] there is x∈[L,R]x \in [L, R]x∈[L,R] such that f(x)=yf(x) = yf(x)=y. Note that, unlike previous paragraphs, the function is not required to be monotonous.

The value xxx could be approximated up to ±δ\pm\delta±δ in O(log⁡R−Lδ)O\left(\log \frac{R-L}{\delta}\right)O(logδR−L​) time for any specific value of δ\deltaδ. The idea is essentially the same, if we take M∈(L,R)M \in (L, R)M∈(L,R) then we would be able to reduce the search interval to either [L,M][L, M][L,M] or [M,R][M, R][M,R] depending on whether f(M)f(M)f(M) is larger than yyy. One common example here would be finding roots of odd-degree polynomials.

For example, let f(x)=x3+ax2+bx+cf(x)=x^3 + ax^2 + bx + cf(x)=x3+ax2+bx+c. Then f(L)→−∞f(L) \to -\inftyf(L)→−∞ and f(R)→+∞f(R) \to +\inftyf(R)→+∞ with L→−∞L \to -\inftyL→−∞ and R→+∞R \to +\inftyR→+∞. Which means that it is always possible to find sufficiently small LLL and sufficiently large RRR such that f(L)<0f(L) < 0f(L)<0 and f(R)>0f(R) > 0f(R)>0. Then, it is possible to find with binary search arbitrarily small interval containing xxx such that f(x)=0f(x)=0f(x)=0.

Search with powers of 2

Another noteworthy way to do binary search is, instead of maintaining an active segment, to maintain the current pointer iii and the current power kkk. The pointer starts at i=Li=Li=L and then on each iteration one tests the predicate at point i+2ki+2^ki+2k. If the predicate is still 000, the pointer is advanced from iii to i+2ki+2^ki+2k, otherwise it stays the same, then the power kkk is decreased by 111.

This paradigm is widely used in tasks around trees, such as finding lowest common ancestor of two vertices or finding an ancestor of a specific vertex that has a certain height. It could also be adapted to e.g. find the kkk-th non-zero element in a Fenwick tree.

Parallel Binary Search

When we are faced with multiple queries that can each be solved with a binary search, it is sometimes too slow to solve them one by one. Parallel Binary Search is a technique that allows us to solve all of these queries simultaneously, often leading to a significant performance improvement. The main idea is to perform the binary search for all queries at the same time (in parallel), step by step. This is particularly effective when the check function for the binary search is costly and can be optimized by processing queries in batches.

Consider a scenario where we have QQQ queries, and for each query qqq, we need to find the smallest value xxx that satisfies a certain condition P(q,x)P(q, x)P(q,x). If P(q,x)P(q, x)P(q,x) is monotonic on xxx, we can use binary search for each query. This would result in a total complexity of O(Q⋅log⁡(range)⋅Tcheck)O(Q \cdot \log(range) \cdot T_{check})O(Q⋅log(range)⋅Tcheck​), where TcheckT_{check}Tcheck​ is the time to evaluate P(q,x)P(q, x)P(q,x).

Parallel binary search optimizes this by changing the order of operations. Instead of processing each query independently, we process all queries simultaneously, step by step. In each step of the binary search, we compute the middle points mim_imi​ for all queries and group the queries by their middle point. This is particularly powerful if the check function P(q,x)P(q, x)P(q,x) has a structure that allows for efficient batching or updates.

Specifically, the major performance gain comes from two scenarios:

  1. Batching expensive checks: If multiple queries need to check the same value mmm in a given step, we can perform the expensive part of the check only once and reuse the result.
  2. Efficiently updatable checks: Often, the check for a value mmm (e.g., "process the first mmm events") can be performed much faster if we have already computed the state for m−1m-1m−1. By processing the check values mmm in increasing order, we can update the state from one check to the next, instead of recomputing from scratch each time. This is a very common pattern in problems involving time or a sequence of updates.

This "offline" processing of queries, where we collect all queries and answer them together in a way that is convenient for our data structures, is the core idea behind parallel binary search.

Implementation

Imagine that we want to answer ZZZ queries about the index of the largest value less than or equal to some XiX_iXi​ (for i=1,2,…,Zi=1,2,\ldots,Zi=1,2,…,Z) in a sorted 0-indexed array AAA. Naturally, each query can be answered using binary search.

Specifically, let us consider the following array A=[1,3,5,7,9,9,13,15]A = [1,3,5,7,9,9,13,15]A=[1,3,5,7,9,9,13,15] with queries: X=[8,11,4,5]X = [8,11,4,5]X=[8,11,4,5]. We can use binary search for each query sequentially.

We generally process this table by columns (queries), but notice that in each row we often repeat access to certain values of the array. To limit access to these values, we can process the table by rows (steps). This does not make huge difference in our small example problem (as we can access all elements in O(1)O(1)O(1)), but in more complex problems, where computing these values is more complicated, this might be essential to solve these problems efficiently. Moreover, note that we can arbitrarily choose the order in which we answer questions in a single row. Let us look at the code implementing this approach.

// Computes the index of the largest value in a sorted array A less than or equal to X_i for all i.
vector<int> parallel_binary_search(vector<int>& A, vector<int>& X) {
    int N = A.size();
    int Z = X.size();
    vector<int> l(Z, -1), r(Z, N);

    for (int step = 1; step <= ceil(log2(N + 1)); ++step) {
        // A vector of vectors to store indices of queries for each middle point.
        vector<vector<int>> m_to_queries(N);

        // Group queries by their middle point.
        for (int i = 0; i < Z; ++i) {
            if (l[i] < r[i] - 1) {
                int m = l[i] + (r[i] - l[i]) / 2;
                m_to_queries[m].push_back(i);
            }
        }

        // Process each group of queries.
        for (int m = 0; m < N; ++m) {
            if (m_to_queries[m].empty()) {
                continue;
            }
            for (int query : m_to_queries[m]) {
                if (X[query] < A[m]) {
                    r[query] = m;
                } else {
                    l[query] = m;
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return l;
}
Example Solution: Meteors

A pretty well known problem using this method is called "Meteors", and is listed in the practice problems. We are given NNN countries, and for each country, a target number of meteors to collect. We are also given a sequence of KKK meteor showers, each affecting a range of countries. The goal is to find, for each country, the earliest time (i.e., which meteor shower) they reach their target.

For a single country, we could binary search for the answer from 111 to KKK. The check for a given time ttt would involve summing up the meteors from the first ttt showers for that country. A naive check takes O(t)O(t)O(t) time, leading to an overall complexity of O(Klog⁡K)O(K \log K)O(KlogK) for one country, and O(N⋅Klog⁡K)O(N \cdot K \log K)O(N⋅KlogK) for all, which is too slow.

With parallel binary search, we search for the answer for all NNN countries at once. In each of the O(log⁡K)O(\log K)O(logK) steps, we have a set of check values tit_iti​ for the countries. We can process these tit_iti​ in increasing order. To perform the check for time ttt, we can use a data structure like a Fenwick tree or a segment tree to maintain the meteor counts for all countries. When moving from checking time tit_iti​ to ti+1t_{i+1}ti+1​, we only need to add the effects of showers from ti+1t_i+1ti​+1 to ti+1t_{i+1}ti+1​ to our data structure. This "update" approach is much faster than recomputing from scratch. The total complexity becomes O((N+K)log⁡Nlog⁡K)O((N+K)\log N \log K)O((N+K)logNlogK).
